```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

normpipe derives norm tables for a questionnaire from a weighted reference
sample. Every norm value comes with a credible band, and every individual
score with an interval on the T metric that accounts for measurement error
and, optionally, for the uncertainty of the norms. This vignette walks
through the steps with the small demo instrument that ships with the package.

```{r}
library(normpipe)
```

## 1. Describe the instrument

An instrument is described by a YAML file: items and their response format,
versions with their scales, reporting cells and a few settings. The demo
instrument has eight items on a seven-point format, two reverse-keyed items,
and a full and a short form.

```{r}
path <- system.file("instruments/demo7/demo7.yml", package = "normpipe")
inst <- read_instrument(path)
inst
```

`scale_registry()` lists every scale. Its `outcome` (`<version>_<scale>`) is
the name used everywhere in the package.

```{r}
scale_registry(inst)
```

All keys of the configuration file are documented in
`vignette("instrument-config")`.

## 2. Reference sample

The reference sample is a list with two data frames: `meta` (`id`, `age`,
`gender`, optionally `weight`) and `items` (the item columns, named
`<prefix><item>`, with the raw response codes). Here it is simulated.

```{r}
sim <- simulate_reference(inst, N = 1500, seed = 2)
head(sim$meta)
head(sim$items)
```

`score_scales()` scores every scale of every version, applying reverse
keying and the scoring rule of each scale.

```{r}
scores <- score_scales(sim$items, inst)
summary(scores$full_b)
```

Design weights can be raked to population margins of the reporting cells
with `make_margins()` and `rake_to_margins()`; `run_norming()` does this
when `margins` is given.

## 3. Norms with norm bands

The norm functions work on a *draw frame*: the scores of the reference
sample, augmented by `prior_mass` pseudo-observations per reporting cell
(a Dirichlet prior over the attainable scores), and replicated over
Bayesian-bootstrap draws of the weights.

```{r}
s <- get_scale(inst, "full_b")
ref <- dplyr::bind_cols(sim$meta, score = scores$full_b)
fr <- direct_frame(ref, s, inst, n_boot = 50)
nm <- weighted_norms(fr, s, inst, cells = character(0))
head(nm[, c("raw", "pctl_med", "pctl_lo", "pctl_hi", "T", "T_lo", "T_hi")])
```

`pctl_med` is the percentile rank (median over draws), `pctl_lo` and
`pctl_hi` its band; `T`, `T_lo` and `T_hi` the same on the T metric,
T = 50 + 10 Φ⁻¹(PR). By default the percentile rank is the midpoint rank
PR = P(X < x) + ½ P(X = x); set `uncertainty: pctl_convention: cumulative`
in the configuration for PR = P(X ≤ x).

`norms_all_cells()` gives the tables for all configured reporting cells
(here gender × age band) plus the overall table, and
`weighted_norms_continuous()` gives kernel-smoothed norms for every year of
age.

### Frequency tables

When only a frequency table is available, `frequency_frame()` builds the
same draw frame from counts per score (and per cell, if the table has
`gender` and `age_group` or `age` columns).

```{r}
freq <- dplyr::count(ref, score, name = "count")
fr_freq <- frequency_frame(freq, s, inst, n_boot = 50)
nm_freq <- weighted_norms(fr_freq, s, inst, cells = character(0))
```

For the same weighted counts, frequency and individual input give identical point norms (`n_boot = 0`) and the same posterior of the norm values.

## 4. Individual intervals

Stage `M1` calibrates an item response model for every scale with
`model: grm` or `model: bifactor` (`fit_scale_model()`, with mirt when it is
installed). From the calibrated model, `conditional_tables()` gives for
every summed score the posterior of the person's trait, mapped onto the T
metric of the reporting cell (score-conditional interval), and
`integrated_intervals()` repeats this under draws of the item parameters and
of the norm values (integrated interval).

## 5. The whole pipeline

`run_norming()` runs all stages and writes the results to a folder. With the
built-in estimator this takes several minutes for the demo instrument; with
mirt it is considerably faster.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
res <- run_norming(inst, ref = list(meta = sim$meta, items = sim$items),
                   out_dir = "demo-out",
                   stages = c("P0", "M1", "M3a", "M3b", "M3c", "M3d", "X1"))
```

The main result is `demo-out/norm_tables_long.csv`, one row per version,
scale, reporting cell and raw score. An example of this table for the demo
instrument is installed with the package:

```{r}
long <- read.csv(system.file("examples/norm_tables_long.csv", package = "normpipe"))
head(long[long$scale == "b" & long$cell == "overall",
          c("raw", "T", "T_lo", "T_hi", "T_cond_lo", "T_cond_hi", "T_int_lo", "T_int_hi")])
```

`T_lo`/`T_hi` is the norm band of the T value, `T_cond_lo`/`T_cond_hi` the
score-conditional interval and `T_int_lo`/`T_int_hi` the integrated interval
of a person with that raw score.

Stages are cached per scale: rerunning `run_norming()` with the same
`out_dir` skips everything that already exists.

## 6. Scales the reference sample did not answer

If the reference sample answered only some items, scales whose items are
all present are normed directly; the others need the transfer module
(stage `M2`). It is configured in the `transfer` block of the instrument and
needs donor samples that answered the full instrument:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
inst <- read_instrument(system.file("instruments/demo7/demo7_transfer.yml",
                                    package = "normpipe"))
inst$donors_data <- list(meta = donor_meta, items = donor_items)  # meta$sample
run_norming(inst, ref = list(meta = ref_meta, items = ref_bridge_items),
            out_dir = "transfer-out", stages = c("P0", "M2", "M3a", "X1"))
```

The transfer models are Bayesian distributional regressions fitted with brms
(backend cmdstanr when installed, otherwise rstan). `scripts/smoke_transfer.R`
in the source repository runs this example end to end on simulated data.
